Prealgebra · Lesson 3.5

GCD and LCM

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Two numbers raise two natural questions. What is the biggest number that divides both of them, and what is the smallest number that both of them divide? The first answer is the GCD and the second is the LCM. The prime fingerprints from 3.3 give you both.

Problem
A maker has ribbons of 56 cm and 70 cm. She wants to cut both into equal whole-centimeter pieces with no scrap. List the divisors of each and find the longest piece length that works for both.
Show a hint
  • A piece length works for a ribbon only if it divides that ribbon's length with nothing left over. So write the divisors of 56 and the divisors of 70, then look for the numbers that show up on both lists.
  • The divisors of 56 are 1,2,4,7,8,14,28,561,2,4,7,8,14,28,56 and the divisors of 70 are 1,2,5,7,10,14,35,701,2,5,7,10,14,35,70. Which numbers sit on both lists, and which of those is biggest?
Show the full solution
A piece length works on a ribbon only if it divides that length evenly, so write out both divisor lists. 56:1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 14, 28, 5656:1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 14, 28, 56 70:1, 2, 5, 10, 7, 14, 35, 7070:1, 2, 5, 10, 7, 14, 35, 70 The numbers on both lists are 1,2,7,1,2,7, and 1414, and the largest is 1414​ centimeters. That gives 56=14×456=14×4 and 70=14×570=14×5, four pieces from one ribbon and five from the other with no scrap.
Problem
Use the fingerprints 168=23×3×7168=23×3×7 and 180=22×32×5180=22×32×5 to find gcd⁡(168,180)gcd(168,180). Take each shared prime to its lower power.
Show a hint
  • Go prime by prime. For the prime 22, the number 168168 carries three of them and 180180 carries two. A divisor of both can lean on at most the smaller count, two. Do the same for 33, and then ask whether 55 or 77 can appear at all.
  • A prime that lives in only one fingerprint cannot divide the other number, so it cannot appear in the gcd. Take each shared prime to the smaller of its two powers, then multiply those together.
Show the full solution
Go prime by prime and keep the smaller power. For 22, that is 2222. For 33, it is 3131. The 55 sits only in 180180 and the 77 only in 168168, so neither can divide both numbers. gcd⁡(168,180)=22×3=12gcd(168,180)=22×3=12​ A common divisor can only use primes both numbers carry, and never more copies than the smaller supply has.
Problem
A volunteer has 90 soap bars and 126 seed packets. Every kit holds the same counts with no leftovers. With gcd⁡(90,126)gcd(90,126), find the greatest number of identical kits she can build.
Show a hint
  • The number of kits must divide 9090 evenly, so the soap splits with none left over, and it must also divide 126126 evenly for the seeds. So the kit count is a common divisor of 9090 and 126126, and she wants the greatest one.
  • Take each shared prime to its lower power. Both numbers carry 22, both carry 3232, but 55 belongs only to 9090 and 77 only to 126126. Multiply the shared part.
Show the full solution
The kit count has to divide both totals evenly, so it is a common divisor of 9090 and 126126, and she wants the greatest one. 90=2×32×5,126=2×32×790=2×32×5,126=2×32×7 Both carry one 22 and both carry 3232, while 55 belongs to 9090 alone and 77 to 126126 alone. gcd⁡(90,126)=2×32=18gcd(90,126)=2×32=18​ Each kit holds 90÷18=590÷18=5 bars and 126÷18=7126÷18=7 packets. Splitting two quantities into as many identical full shares as possible is always a gcd question.
Key idea
The greatest common divisor gcd(a,b), also called the greatest common factor, is the largest number that divides both a and b with nothing left over. Every pair has 1 as a common divisor, and no number has a divisor larger than itself, so a single greatest one always exists. Compare the two prime factorizations. The gcd uses each shared prime raised to the lower of its two powers, because a common divisor can only use primes that both numbers have, and only as many copies of each as both numbers have. A prime that appears in only one factorization is left out. When two numbers share no prime at all, their only common divisor is 1, and we call them coprime.
Problem
Two gears have 24 and 35 teeth, with 24=23×324=23×3 and 35=5×735=5×7. They share no prime factor. How many teeth must pass the meshing point before the red teeth touch again?
Show a hint
  • The red teeth realign after a count of teeth that both 2424 and 3535 divide evenly, so you want the smallest number that is a multiple of both. Start listing multiples of 3535 and check which is the first that 2424 also divides.
  • Because 2424 and 3535 share no prime factor, a number divisible by both must carry all of 2424's primes and all of 3535's primes with no overlap to save on. The smallest such number is just 24×3524×35.
Show the full solution
The red teeth meet again at the first tooth count both gears divide evenly. Since 24=23×324=23×3 and 35=5×735=5×7 share no prime, a number divisible by both has to carry all four primes, and the smallest one that does is their product. 24×35=84024×35=840​ That is 3535 full turns of the 2424-tooth gear and 2424 of the 3535-tooth one. Coprime numbers have nothing to share, so their lcm is just the two multiplied together.

That problem was the second question, the smallest count that both numbers divide evenly. When two numbers share no factors, that count is just their product. When they do share factors, it comes out smaller.

Problem
Two beacons flash every 9 seconds and every 12 seconds. List the flash times and find the first second after the start when both flash together.
Show a hint
  • The first beacon flashes at the multiples of 99, the second at the multiples of 1212. You want the first number that shows up on both lists of multiples.
  • Multiples of 99 are 9,18,27,36,45,…9,18,27,36,45,… and multiples of 1212 are 12,24,36,48,…12,24,36,48,…. What is the smallest number appearing on both?
Show the full solution
The first beacon flashes at the multiples of 99 and the second at the multiples of 1212, so walk both lists. 9:9, 18, 27, 36, 45, …9:9, 18, 27, 36, 45, … 12:12, 24, 36, 48, …12:12, 24, 36, 48, … The first number on both is second 3636​, where one beacon has flashed four times and the other three. That beats 9×12=1089×12=108 because 99 and 1212 share a factor of 33 that does not need counting twice.
Problem
Use 168=23×3×7168=23×3×7 and 180=22×32×5180=22×32×5 to find lcm⁡(168,180)lcm(168,180). Take each prime to its higher power, including primes in only one fingerprint.
Show a hint
  • Go prime by prime again, but this time take the larger demand. For 22, the number 168168 wants 2323 while 180180 only wants 2222, so the lcm must supply 2323 to satisfy 168168. Do the same for every prime that appears in either number.
  • Every prime in either fingerprint must appear in the lcm, each to the highest power demanded by either number. Collect 2323, 3232, 55, and 77, then multiply.
Show the full solution
A number that both 168168 and 180180 divide has to meet the larger demand for every prime. For 22 that is 2323, from 168168. For 33 it is 3232, from 180180. The 55 and the 77 each show up in only one number but still have to appear. lcm⁡(168,180)=23×32×5×7=8×9×5×7=2520lcm(168,180)=23×32×5×7=8×9×5×7=2520​ Check that 2520=168×15=180×142520=168×15=180×14. The lcm takes each prime to the higher power, the mirror of the gcd taking the lower.
Problem
Three subway lines depart every 12, 18, and 30 minutes. Build lcm⁡(12,18,30)lcm(12,18,30) from the fingerprints and report how many minutes until all three lines next leave together.
Show a hint
  • Each line departs at the multiples of its own period, so all three leave together at a common multiple of 1212, 1818, and 3030. You want the smallest such number, the least common multiple of all three.
  • Write 12=22×312=22×3, 18=2×3218=2×32, and 30=2×3×530=2×3×5. For each prime that appears, take the highest power any of the three numbers demands, then multiply.
Show the full solution
All three lines leave together at the common multiples of 1212, 1818, and 3030, so take each prime to the highest power any of the three demands. 12=22×3,18=2×32,30=2×3×512=22×3,18=2×32,30=2×3×5 That is 2222 from 1212, 3232 from 1818, and 55 from 3030. lcm⁡(12,18,30)=22×32×5=4×9×5=180lcm(12,18,30)=22×32×5=4×9×5=180​ And indeed 180=12×15=18×10=30×6180=12×15=18×10=30×6. The rule stretches to any number of values, always the highest power demanded by any of them.
Key idea
The least common multiple lcm(a,b) is the smallest positive number that both a and b divide evenly. Two events that repeat every a steps and every b steps happen together at the common multiples of a and b, and the first of those is their lcm. There is no greatest common multiple, since every pair has infinitely many common multiples. Compare the two prime factorizations. The lcm takes every prime to the higher of its two powers, because a common multiple must contain every prime either number has, in at least the amount that number uses. Every prime from either factorization appears, and no others do.
Problem
A locksmith knows two numbers have gcd⁡=8gcd=8 and lcm⁡=240lcm=240, and one number is 48. Use the relationship gcd⁡×lcm⁡=a×bgcd×lcm=a×b to find the other number.
Show a hint
  • Try multiplying a few pairs of numbers and comparing the product to the gcd times the lcm of the same pair. For example take 1212 and 1818: their product is 216216, their gcd is 66, and their lcm is 3636. What do you notice about 6×366×36?
  • For any two numbers, the gcd times the lcm equals the two numbers multiplied together. So here 48×(other)=8×24048×(other)=8×240. Solve for the other number.
Show the full solution
For any pair, gcd⁡×lcm⁡=a×bgcd×lcm=a×b, so the two numbers multiply to 8×240=19208×240=1920. Dividing out the known one, other=192048=40other=481920​=40​ Checking, 48=24×348=24×3 and 40=23×540=23×5 share 23=823=8, and their lcm is 24×3×5=24024×3×5=240. The rule holds because for each prime the gcd takes the lower power and the lcm takes the higher, so between them they use exactly the two powers the numbers had.
Key idea
For any two whole numbers, gcd(a,b) × lcm(a,b) = a × b. For each prime the gcd took the lower power and the lcm took the higher power, so between them they use exactly the two powers the original numbers had, and multiplying across all primes gives back a × b. Rearranged, lcm(a,b) = (a × b)/(gcd(a,b)), so knowing any three of the four numbers gives the fourth.
Problem
Dividing marbles into groups of 4, 6, or 9 always leaves exactly 1 over. What is the smallest number of marbles greater than 1 that behaves this way?
Show a hint
  • If you set the one leftover marble aside, the rest divide perfectly into groups of 44, of 66, and of 99. So the count minus 11 is a common multiple of 44, 66, and 99.
  • The smallest number that 44, 66, and 99 all divide is lcm⁡(4,6,9)lcm(4,6,9). Find it, then add back the single leftover marble.
  • With 4=224=22, 6=2×36=2×3, and 9=329=32, the lcm is 22×32=3622×32=36. The marble count is one more than the smallest common multiple above zero.
Show the full solution
Lift the one leftover marble away and what remains divides evenly into groups of 44, of 66, and of 99, so the count minus 11 is a common multiple of all three. 4=22,6=2×3,9=32,lcm⁡(4,6,9)=22×32=364=22,6=2×3,9=32,lcm(4,6,9)=22×32=36 Put the stranded marble back and the count is 36+1=3736+1=37​. A number leaving the same remainder under several divisors sits that fixed step above a common multiple, so the smallest one is the lcm plus the remainder.
Key idea
When a number leaves the same remainder r under several divisors, subtract r and what is left divides all of them evenly, so it is a common multiple and the smallest such number is lcm+r. When each remainder is one less than its divisor, the number is one short of dividing cleanly, so it is one below a common multiple and the smallest is lcm-1. In both cases the answer comes from the multiples of a single lcm.
Problem
A bakery wants the smallest four-digit batch number divisible by 6, 8, and 9 at once. Find lcm⁡(6,8,9)lcm(6,8,9), then find its smallest four-digit multiple.
Show a hint
  • A number divisible by 66, 88, and 99 is exactly a common multiple of the three, so the ones that qualify are the multiples of lcm⁡(6,8,9)lcm(6,8,9). Find that lcm first.
  • With 6=2×36=2×3, 8=238=23, and 9=329=32, the lcm is 23×32=7223×32=72. Now find the smallest four-digit multiple of 7272 by dividing 10001000 by 7272 and rounding up.
Show the full solution
Divisible by 66, 88, and 99 at once means being a multiple of their lcm. 6=2×3,8=23,9=32,lcm⁡(6,8,9)=23×32=726=2×3,8=23,9=32,lcm(6,8,9)=23×32=72 Since 1000÷72≈13.91000÷72≈13.9, thirteen 7272s land at 936936, still three digits, so the next multiple is the first to clear the line. 72×14=100872×14=1008​ Hitting several divisors at once collapses the search into one list, the multiples of a single number.
Problem
Two pendulums swing every 21 and 28 seconds (21=3×721=3×7, 28=22×728=22×7). Find their lcm, then count how many times both start a swing together in the first 600 seconds.
Show a hint
  • The first pendulum starts a swing at the multiples of 2121, the second at the multiples of 2828. They begin together exactly at the common multiples of 2121 and 2828, which are the multiples of lcm⁡(21,28)lcm(21,28). Find that lcm first.
  • With 21=3×721=3×7 and 28=22×728=22×7, the lcm is 22×3×7=8422×3×7=84. Now count how many multiples of 8484 land in the window from just after 00 up to 600600.
  • Count the whole multiples of 8484 that are at most 600600. Since 84×7=58884×7=588 and 84×8=67284×8=672, see how many steps of 8484 fit before passing 600600.
Show the full solution
The pendulums start together at the common multiples of 2121 and 2828, which are the multiples of their lcm. 21=3×7,28=22×7,lcm⁡(21,28)=22×3×7=8421=3×7,28=22×7,lcm(21,28)=22×3×7=84 Stepping by 8484 gives 84,168,252,336,420,504,58884,168,252,336,420,504,588, and the next would be 672672, past 600600. That is 77​ shared starts. Counting coincidences in a window is just counting multiples of one number, the lcm of the two periods.
Fun fact
Euclid computed gcd without factoring. Divide the larger by the smaller, keep the remainder, repeat until the remainder is zero. The last nonzero remainder is the gcd. Computers still use this today.

Both ideas come from the same two fingerprints. The overlap gives the gcd, everything across both gives the lcm, and gcd⁡×lcm⁡=a×bgcd×lcm=a×b ties them together. The common multiples of a pair are exactly the multiples of their lcm, which sends you back to the multiple counting of 3.1.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Find gcd⁡(120,144)gcd(120,144) using 120=23×3×5120=23×3×5 and 144=24×32144=24×32. Take each shared prime to its lower power.
Show the solution
Keep each shared prime at its lower power. For 22 that is 2323, and for 33 it is 3131. The 55 appears only in 120120, so it contributes nothing. gcd⁡(120,144)=23×3=24gcd(120,144)=23×3=24​ Check that 120=24×5120=24×5 and 144=24×6144=24×6, both whole.
Practice
Using 120=23×3×5120=23×3×5 and 144=24×32144=24×32, find lcm⁡(120,144)lcm(120,144) by taking each prime to its higher power.
Show the solution
Take each prime to its higher power, including one carried by just a single number. For 22 that is 2424, for 33 it is 3232, and the 55 from 120120 has to come along. lcm⁡(120,144)=24×32×5=16×9×5=720lcm(120,144)=24×32×5=16×9×5=720​ The gcd was 2424, and 24×720=17280=120×14424×720=17280=120×144, exactly as gcd⁡×lcm⁡=a×bgcd×lcm=a×b promises.
Practice
With 49=7249=72 and 60=22×3×560=22×3×5, do these numbers share any prime factor? Report their greatest common divisor.
Show the solution
49=7249=72 is built only from 77, and 60=22×3×560=22×3×5 carries no 77 at all. With no prime in common, the only number dividing both is 11​. Two numbers that share no prime are called coprime, and their gcd is always 11.
Practice
Two numbers have gcd⁡=9gcd=9 and lcm⁡=270lcm=270. One number is 45. Find the other.
Show the solution
Since gcd⁡×lcm⁡=a×bgcd×lcm=a×b, the two numbers multiply to 9×270=24309×270=2430. Dividing out the known one, other=243045=54other=452430​=54​ Checking, 45=32×545=32×5 and 54=2×3354=2×33 share 32=932=9, and their lcm is 2×33×5=2702×33×5=270.
Practice
Two ferries leave together and return every 16 and 24 minutes. How many minutes until both depart together again?
Show the solution
The ferries leave together at the common multiples of 1616 and 2424, and the first one is their lcm. 16=24,24=23×3,lcm⁡(16,24)=24×3=4816=24,24=23×3,lcm(16,24)=24×3=48​ Check that 48=16×3=24×248=16×3=24×2, both whole.
Practice
Stacking badges leaves 1 over for groups of 5, 6, or 8. What is the smallest badge count greater than 1 with this property?
Show the solution
Set the leftover badge aside and the rest divides evenly into stacks of 55, 66, and 88, so the count minus 11 is a common multiple of the three. With 6=2×36=2×3 and 8=238=23, lcm⁡(5,6,8)=23×3×5=120.lcm(5,6,8)=23×3×5=120. Adding the badge back gives 120+1=121120+1=121​. Check that 121=5×24+1=6×20+1=8×15+1121=5×24+1=6×20+1=8×15+1.
Practice
Two readings of two fingerprints. The gcd takes each shared prime to its lower power, and the lcm takes every prime to its higher power. They satisfy gcd⁡×lcm⁡=a×bgcd×lcm=a×b. Common multiples are multiples of the lcm.
Practice
Two rhythms of 9 and 12 beats loop together. Find the largest common multiple of 9 and 12 below 300.
Show the solution
A loop that is a whole number of both rhythms is a common multiple of 99 and 1212, so it is a multiple of their lcm. 9=32,12=22×3,lcm⁡(9,12)=22×32=369=32,12=22×3,lcm(9,12)=22×32=36 Since 300÷36≈8.3300÷36≈8.3, the largest multiple staying under 300300 is 36×8=28836×8=288​, and the next one, 324324, sails past. The common multiples of two numbers are exactly the multiples of their lcm, so a hunt like this only ever scans one list.
Practice
A poster shop prints only in runs divisible by 4, 5, and 6 at once. Find lcm⁡(4,5,6)lcm(4,5,6) and its smallest three-digit multiple.
Show the solution
A run divisible by all three is a common multiple of 44, 55, and 66, so it is a multiple of their lcm. 4=22,5=5,6=2×3,lcm⁡(4,5,6)=22×3×5=604=22,5=5,6=2×3,lcm(4,5,6)=22×3×5=60 The multiples of 6060 run 60,120,180,…60,120,180,…, and the first with three digits is 120120​. Check that 120=4×30=5×24=6×20120=4×30=5×24=6×20.
Practice
Two lights flash every 10 and 15 seconds. In 300 seconds after the start, how many times do both flash together?
Show the solution
The lights coincide at the common multiples of 1010 and 1515, which are the multiples of their lcm. 10=2×5,15=3×5,lcm⁡(10,15)=2×3×5=3010=2×5,15=3×5,lcm(10,15)=2×3×5=30 So they flash together every 3030 seconds, and 300÷30=10300÷30=10​ of those land in the window, at 30,60,9030,60,90, on up to 300300.
Practice
A crowd leaves 1 person over for teams of 2, 3, 4, or 5. What is the smallest crowd greater than 1 with this property?
Show the solution
Set the leftover person aside and the rest splits evenly into teams of 22, 33, 44, and 55, so the crowd minus 11 is a common multiple of all four. lcm⁡(2,3,4,5)=22×3×5=60lcm(2,3,4,5)=22×3×5=60 Adding that person back gives 60+1=6160+1=61​. Check that 6161 leaves exactly 11 over for each of the four team sizes.
Practice
A wall is 132 cm by 198 cm. Using 132=22×3×11132=22×3×11 and 198=2×32×11198=2×32×11, find the side length of the largest square tile that fits exactly.
Show the solution
A tile of side ss fits exactly only when ss divides both 132132 and 198198, so the largest tile is the gcd. Each shared prime goes to its lower power, giving one 22, one 33, and one 1111. gcd⁡(132,198)=2×3×11=66gcd(132,198)=2×3×11=66​ The tile is 6666 cm on a side, fitting 22 across and 33 up. The largest square that tiles a whole-number rectangle is always the gcd of the two sides.
Practice
A number leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, remainder 5 when divided by 6, and remainder 7 when divided by 8. Notice each remainder is one less than its divisor. What is the smallest such number?
Show the solution
Each remainder is one less than its divisor, so adding 11 would make the number divide evenly by 44, 66, and 88 at once. That puts it one below a common multiple. 4=22,6=2×3,8=23,lcm⁡(4,6,8)=23×3=244=22,6=2×3,8=23,lcm(4,6,8)=23×3=24 So the number is 24−1=2324−1=23​. Check that 23=4×5+3=6×3+5=8×2+723=4×5+3=6×3+5=8×2+7.
Practice
GCD and LCM are the engines of fractions. Reducing divides by the gcd, and adding different-denominator fractions uses the lcm as common denominator. Master these now and fraction work becomes routine.
